summary:
The Covariance calculator works out the answer. It uses the observation 1 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)), the observation 2 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)), the observation 3 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)) and the observation 4 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)).

It is built for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Covariance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Covariance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the observation 1 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)), the observation 2 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)), the observation 3 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)) and the observation 4 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Covariance calculator
sections.html:
This one is not a single closed-form equation. It is driven by a page script that applies a set of rules — lookups, cut-offs and conditional branches — and the numbers you see are the script's output rather than the rearrangement of one line of algebra. The rules are what make the tool useful: a plain formula cannot express a table of thresholds or a choice between cases.

Practically, that means you can trust the result but cannot reproduce it with a pocket calculator. If you need to show your working, quote the inputs and the output rather than an equation.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Covariance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the observation 1 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)), the observation 2 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)) and the observation 3 (First sample (enter up to 30 values)) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Covariance calculator?
faq.a: The form has 60 fields, each listed with its unit in the article above. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Is the Covariance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.

faq.q: Does it work in both directions?
faq.a: Where the maths allows it, yes: the page states which values it solves for and which you supply. A field marked as a result is always computed, never typed into.
